Summary and Source: Argentina signed a U.S.-Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment (ARTI), with the labor commitment finalized around Feb 5, 2026: Argentina committed to "adopt and implement a prohibition on the importation of goods produced by forced or compulsory labor," placing it in USTR's lower 10% tariff tier. This was directly verified against the USTR fact sheet. No domestic Argentine bill or implementing regulation has been found tabled yet -- this is a treaty-level commitment only, structurally the same situation as Jordan's Article 2.9 commitment, and is reclassified from "No" to "Partial" for consistency with that precedent. No Argentina-specific hearing testimony found in the July 7-9 hearing record. Source: USTR fact sheet, Nov 2025/Feb 2026; White & Case / Gibson Dunn (law firm summaries of USTR determination). Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (U.S.-Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment: Argentina commits to adopt and implement a forced-labor import prohibition; treaty-level commitment only, no domestic bill/regulation tabled yet -- reclassified from No to Partial for consistency with Jordan's equivalent RTA-commitment-only precedent)

Summary and Source: Trade Minister Don Farrell rejected USTR's finding, calling the tariffs "unjustified and inconsistent" with the US-Australia FTA and asserting Australia already has "world-leading" modern slavery legislation; Australia also submitted written comments to USTR ahead of the July hearings. On July 16, 2026, the federal government announced it intends to introduce reforms to the Modern Slavery Act 2018 centered on a new criminal "failure to prevent" modern slavery offence for companies with over AUD 100 million revenue; this remains an announcement of intent only -- no bill has been tabled in Parliament -- and it would in any case be a corporate-liability offence, not an import prohibition. STALE-SOURCE GUARD (re-confirmed this run): search results periodically surface a headline that the Australian Senate "passed" a forced-labour import bill. That refers to Senator Rex Patrick's 2021/2022 private senator's bill, which lapsed before the 2022 election and never became law. It must not be treated as a current or enacted measure. Source: HCAMag / SBS News, June 3, 2026; Baker McKenzie, July 2026; Walk Free, July 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Australia, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (Modern Slavery Act 2018 is a reporting regime, not an import prohibition; the announced "failure to prevent" offence is unlegislated and corporate-liability in nature, and the 2021 Senate private member's bill lapsed)

Summary and Source: The Customs Management (Amendment) Bill 2026 passed the House of Assembly alongside the 2026-2027 Budget, and the Bahamas government's own legislation portal lists it by name under "Tabled in House of Assembly." Operative text (from The Tribune's reporting of the Bill, July 24, 2026): new section 208A provides that "The Minister may, by Order, prohibit the importation of any goods, wholly or partially produced or manufactured, from any supplier, country or territory if there are reasonable grounds to believe that the goods are a result of forced labour," with objects and reasons aimed at "prohibiting goods from suppliers, places or countries that produce forced (child) labour from entering The Bahamas" -- so if enacted it would be a DESIGNATION-DEPENDENT framework ban, like Trinidad and Tobago's Customs Act s.45(1)(w) and India's FTP Para 2.20B, not a self-executing prohibition. ENACTMENT RE-VERIFIED AUGUST 9, 2026: the anti-bot block that defeated every attempt on August 7 and 8 cleared, and the 2026 Acts-by-Year register was retrieved and parsed successfully -- 18 enacted Acts, still current through Act No. 2026-0038 (Environmental Health Services (Amendment) Act), with NO Customs Management amendment among them. That is a sixth successful verification of non-enactment from the government's own record. Tooling note retained for future runs: this register intermittently returns an HTTP 202 sgcaptcha challenge, and a failed fetch is NOT evidence in either direction -- it must be retrieved successfully before any conclusion is drawn. No source has ever reported Senate passage or the Governor-General's assent. Source: The Tribune (Bahamas), July 24, 27 and 28, 2026; Government of The Bahamas legislation portal (tabled register and Acts-by-Year register, re-verified August 9, 2026).
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (Customs Management (Amendment) Bill 2026, new s.208A empowering the Minister to prohibit forced-labour imports by Order -- a designation-dependent framework ban; passed by the House of Assembly with the 2026-2027 Budget, with no Senate passage or assent ever reported; the government's 2026 Acts-by-Year register, re-verified August 9, 2026 and current through Act No. 2026-0038, contains no Customs Management amendment)

No implementing import-ban law found yet, so this remains a treaty-level commitment only -- the same situation as Jordan's Article 2.9 commitment -- and is reclassified from "No" to "Partial" for consistency. Source: USTR Fact Sheet (US-Bangladesh ART), Feb 2026; Dhaka Tribune, June 3, 2026; ESG Institute Bangladesh, 2026. Summary and Source: STATUS CHANGE this run, No to Partial -- a policy-consistency correction, not a new event. Brazil has had a formally tabled forced-labour import-ban bill since 2015: PL 2.799/2015 (Dep. Davidson Magalhaes), which with PL 3717/2015 and PL 5072/2016 attached would prohibit importing and trading goods made with child, forced or compulsory labour, provide for seizure and forfeiture, and require the government to publish a six-monthly list of implicated companies drawing on ILO data and court decisions. Verified directly against the Chamber of Deputies' own tramitacao record (dadosabertos.camara.leg.br, 76 recorded events): the Labour Committee approved the rapporteur's substitutive on September 15, 2025 -- which expanded the original cocoa-only text to all products -- the Economic Development Committee (CDE) approved its parecer on June 10, 2026, and the bill was received by the Constitution, Justice and Citizenship Committee (CCJC) on June 12, 2026, where it is awaiting designation of a rapporteur. It is not enacted and still requires CCJC and Senate passage. Under the standing policy a formally tabled but unenacted import-ban bill is Partial, so the prior "No" was inconsistent with the classification rule rather than with the facts. Two dating corrections recorded: the CDE approval was June 10, 2026, not "the week of July 13" as this row previously stated, and the widely syndicated "committee approves" article is the Chamber's own September 15, 2025 story about the Labour Committee, not a 2026 item. Separately, Brazil's government (gov.br/Secom) called USTR's conclusion "regrettable," citing its ILO-recognised record; and a distinct, unrelated 25% Section 301 tariff (digital trade, ethanol, deforestation, IP) took effect July 22, 2026, on top of which the 12.5% forced-labour tariff was confirmed July 23, 2026. Source: Camara dos Deputados open-data tramitacao record and Camara news, September 15, 2025; gov.br/Secom; USTR press release, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (PL 2.799/2015, with PL 3717/2015 and PL 5072/2016 attached, would prohibit importing and trading goods made with child/forced labour; substitutive approved by the Labour Committee September 15, 2025 and by the Economic Development Committee June 10, 2026, received by the Constitution and Justice Committee June 12, 2026 awaiting a rapporteur; not enacted, still requires CCJC and Senate passage)

Summary and Source: Canada has had a forced-labor import prohibition since July 1, 2020 (Customs Tariff item 9897.00.00) but USTR flagged weak enforcement (only 2 shipments ever actually prohibited). In response, Canada tabled Bill C-35 -- "An Act respecting the prohibition of the importation of goods produced by forced labour" -- on June 12, 2026, to strengthen the ban with a new supply-chain tracing framework. STAGE CLARIFIED this run against Parliament's own LegisInfo record, because it is easy to misread: the bill's status field reads "At second reading in the House of Commons," but its latest recorded event is still "Introduction and first reading" dated June 12, 2026, and its latest COMPLETED major stage is First reading. Under LegisInfo's convention the status names the stage a bill is awaiting, not one it has cleared -- so C-35 has NOT advanced, and no second-reading debate has occurred, with Parliament in summer recess. A future run should not read that status label as progress. The Global Affairs Canada/CBSA consultation on forced-labour import identification criteria and importer evidentiary requirements, and a parallel ESDC supply-chain due-diligence consultation, remain open and CLOSE AUGUST 21, 2026, with no "what we heard" report yet. Canada also submitted written comments reiterating there is "no basis" for additional Section 301 duties. Canada stays Yes under the standing carve-out: an enacted ban in force is not downgraded by a separate pending strengthening bill. Source: Parliament of Canada LegisInfo (primary, checked directly); Global Affairs Canada, June 12 and July 27, 2026. USTR's final determination of July 23, 2026 confirmed a 10% tariff for Canada.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (existing ban since 2020; Bill C-35 introduced June 12, 2026 and still only at first reading -- its LegisInfo status label "At second reading" denotes the stage awaited, not one completed -- with Global Affairs Canada/CBSA and ESDC consultations open until August 21, 2026)

Summary and Source: China's Ministry of Commerce called USTR's final action "typical unilateralism and protectionism" (July 27, 2026), noted that the US itself has not ratified ILO Forced Labour Convention No. 29, and pointed to China's own labour-law framework and its ratification of 28 ILO conventions. ESCALATION this run: after DHS added 43 Chinese companies to the UFLPA Entity List on July 31 (taking it from 144 to 187 entities, effective August 3, 2026, published as Federal Register notice 2026-15628), MOFCOM moved from verbal condemnation -- calling the listing "completely groundless" and "economic coercion" -- to ACTUAL COUNTERMEASURES on August 5, 2026: tightened export controls on drones, their key components and related technologies bound for the United States, which now face strict case-by-case review with license-facilitation measures withdrawn, plus suspension of part of China-US product-certification cooperation. No retaliatory tariff has been announced, and reporting attributes the restraint partly to a planned Xi-Trump summit. CLASSIFICATION UNCHANGED: these are retaliatory trade-control measures and the UFLPA listing is a US enforcement action -- neither is a Chinese forced-labour import prohibition, and Chinese-language searches continue to find no PRC import-ban law. Source: MOFCOM, July 27 and August 5, 2026; Global Times, August 1 and August 2026; US Department of Homeland Security, July 31, 2026; Federal Register 2026-15628.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No

Summary and Source: Colombia published a draft MinCIT resolution on July 15, 2026 to prohibit forced-labour imports, but it was never issued, and a competence standoff between MinCIT and the DIAN over which body holds the authority has blocked it. NEW this run: Colombia underwent a government transition at end-July/early-August 2026, and the incoming Commerce Minister, Jose Manuel Restrepo, announced on July 24 a set of "first measures" including working tables ("mesas de trabajo") with the United States from July 28 aimed at producing a draft decree on forced-labour import controls. Separately the outgoing government issued Decreto 552 de 2026 setting business-and-human-rights guidelines for executive-branch entities -- general due-diligence guidance, NOT an import prohibition, and it does not affect this classification. MinCIT's own 2026 decree registry was re-checked directly on August 8 and still runs only to Decreto No. 0731 (July 8, a soybean tariff-classification matter unrelated to forced labour), so no decree or resolution has been issued and the DIAN/MinCIT standoff remains unresolved under the new administration. Source: MinCIT decree registry (government, checked directly); El Tiempo and Infobae, July 24, 2026; El Colombiano and El Heraldo, July 24-27, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (draft MinCIT resolution published July 15, 2026 but never issued; MinCIT/DIAN competence standoff unresolved, and MinCIT's own decree registry still shows no forced-labour decree as of August 8, 2026; the incoming Commerce Minister has committed to working tables with the US toward a draft decree, but nothing further has been published)

Summary and Source: President Abinader issued Decreto num. 502-26 on July 23, 2026 -- the day the 12.5% US tariff took effect -- establishing an administrative procedure empowering the Direccion General de Aduanas (DGA), coordinated with the Labor Ministry, Public Ministry, Industry and Commerce and Foreign Affairs, to identify, restrict and prohibit importation of merchandise produced wholly or partly with forced labor. The decree creates a public registry of prohibited products and lets DGA preventively retain or bar suspect goods including consignments already in transit or sitting at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies. DATE DISCREPANCY RESOLVED this run: at least one secondary outlet (Revista Mercado) dates the decree to June 23, 2026; the Presidency's own decree page for 502-26 carries 23 de Julio 2026, so the July 23 date recorded here is confirmed against the primary source and the June date is incorrect. The private sector has raised implementation concerns and commentators question enforcement capacity; no implementing regulation has been issued and no enforcement action has yet been identified. Source: Presidencia de la Republica Dominicana (primary, decree page re-verified August 3, 2026); Diario Libre, July 23 and 26, 2026; El Nuevo Diario.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto No. 502-26, issued July 23, 2026 -- date confirmed against the Presidency's own decree page; establishes a public registry of prohibited products and empowers customs (DGA) to preventively retain and bar forced-labor-linked merchandise, including goods already in transit or at port, with re-export or destruction as remedies)

Summary and Source: Ecuador holds the 10% tier on the basis of COMEX Resolution 005-2026, which created the inter-institutional technical team (ETITF, spanning the Production Ministry, customs authority SENAE and the Labour Ministry) to restrict imports of forced-labor-produced goods; USTR credits the measure but assesses enforcement as weak, and no enforcement action has been identified. Production Minister Luis Alberto Jaramillo reiterated at USA Trade Connect 2026 in Guayaquil (July 28) that Ecuador "complies with its commitments and controls." New detail this run: the separate US-Ecuador Reciprocal Trade Agreement signed March 13, 2026 is NOT yet in force -- it still requires Constitutional Court review and National Assembly approval -- and Ecuador has a 12-month window to stand up its compliance systems. Ecuador's Yes therefore rests on the enacted COMEX resolution, not the unratified RTA. Source: El Universo and Primicias, July 2026; Ministerio de Produccion.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (COMEX Resolution 005-2026 establishing the inter-institutional mechanism restricting forced-labor-linked imports; USTR assesses enforcement as weak. The separate US-Ecuador RTA signed March 13, 2026 is not yet in force -- it still requires Constitutional Court review and National Assembly approval)

Summary and Source: USTR credits the EU with an enacted prohibition but assesses enforcement as inadequate because Regulation (EU) 2024/3015 is not applicable until December 14, 2027. Article 3 verified directly from EUR-Lex: "Economic operators shall not place or make available on the Union market products that are made with forced labour, nor shall they export such products." The Regulation is marked "(Text with EEA relevance)," the basis for Norway's incorporation, and Article 2(1) defines forced labour by reference to ILO Convention No. 29. The Commission's implementation guidelines of June 26, 2026 (C(2026) 4386 final) and the Forced Labour Single Portal are confirmed on the Commission's own initiative page, with implementation-readiness webinars scheduled from September 2026. NEW this run and verified directly against EUR-Lex: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/903 of 24 April 2026, adopted under Article 7(7)(a) of Reg. 2024/3015, specifies the details and functionalities of the information and communication system for the Regulation -- a dedicated forced-labour module within ICSMS (the market-surveillance system under Reg. (EU) 2019/1020), used for the general-provisions, investigations, decisions and enforcement chapters and for data exchange between the Commission, national competent authorities and customs. Its Article 11 provides that it enters into force on the twentieth day following publication in the Official Journal (secondary reporting puts that at May 17, 2026; the OJ publication date was not independently confirmed). All of this is machinery for a still-inapplicable prohibition, so classification is unchanged. Source: EUR-Lex (primary texts of Reg. 2024/3015 and Implementing Reg. 2026/903); European Commission initiative 16292 and C(2026) 4386 final, June 26, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Regulation (EU) 2024/3015, Article 3 prohibition, in force but not applicable until December 14, 2027; Commission implementation guidelines adopted June 26, 2026, Forced Labour Single Portal live, and Implementing Reg. (EU) 2026/903 of 24 April 2026 establishing the ICSMS forced-labour module)

Summary and Source: Guatemala's Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026 (published July 6, 2026) secured it the 10% tier. ENTRY-INTO-FORCE DATE STILL CONTESTED -- a correction to this row's framing yesterday, which called the question resolved. Agexport (the exporters' chamber) and Prensa Libre both describe a 30-BUSINESS-day period from publication, which counts to approximately AUGUST 17, 2026. But DataExport states the agreement entered into force in EARLY AUGUST, and AGN reads it as effective on or within 30 calendar days of publication. No source reports an actual, dated entry-into-force event, and the primary Acuerdo text remains unretrievable (dca.gob.gt returns 403 on every attempt across many runs), so the day-count cannot be settled against the instrument itself. The row therefore records the ~August 17 business-day reading as the best-supported of the three, while stating plainly that it is contested secondary reporting rather than a verified figure. Scope is narrower than early reporting implied: rather than a blanket product or origin prohibition, it bars imports from a specific list of foreign companies. MINTRAB says it lacks extraterritorial investigative capacity and will build that list from formal foreign retention orders and diplomatic-channel information plus US Department of Labor data; the ~90-day list window runs from entry into force, and a MINTRAB official said in late July that the "next 90 days" would be used to build the operational roadmap, implying the clock had not yet started. No list has been published. Classification stays Yes because the instrument is formally published by the competent authority, which the standing policy treats as enactment even before effectiveness. Source: Agexport and Prensa Libre, July 2026; DataExport; AGN; La Hora, July 15, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Acuerdo Ministerial 377-2026, published July 6, 2026; entry into force reported variously as ~August 17, 2026 on a 30-business-day count (Agexport, Prensa Libre) or early August (DataExport), with no dated entry-into-force event reported and the primary text unretrievable, so the date is contested secondary reporting; scope limited to a company-specific list MINTRAB has not yet published)

Summary and Source: Honduras testified at the July 7 USTR hearing (Melvin Redondo, Presidential Office of Foreign Trade), announcing an executive decree creating an express legal prohibition on importing forced-labor-made goods with three enforcement mechanisms (importer declarations, a Ministry of Labour risk list, and binding customs opinions), and requested a 10% "bridge rate" pending completion of its own Reciprocal Trade Agreement. Honduras's Council of Ministers, under President Nasry "Tito" Asfura, approved the executive decree the night of July 16, 2026; it was published the next day as Decreto Ejecutivo No. PCM-014-2026 in La Gaceta No. 37,196 (July 17, 2026), citing ILO Conventions 29/105 and CAFTA-DR obligations. The decree (Art. 4) prohibits importing goods produced wholly or partly with forced/compulsory labor, takes effect on publication, and directs Customs to build the prohibited-goods list into its risk-management system (Art. 7: intercepted goods face re-export or destruction at importer cost). TIMELINE REFINED this run against the decree text on leyes.hn: the Labour Ministry's implementing ministerial agreement and prohibited-goods list are due within 30 calendar days of entry into force (~August 16, 2026), and enforcement then begins a further 30 days after THAT list is published in the Diario Oficial -- so actual enforcement is a two-step runway, not a single deadline. Re-checked August 5, 2026: neither the implementing agreement nor the list has been published. Near-term watch item. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026; La Gaceta (official gazette) No. 37,196, July 17, 2026, and the decree text via leyes.hn. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 10% for Honduras, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto Ejecutivo PCM-014-2026, published in La Gaceta No. 37,196, July 17, 2026; effective on publication, with the Labour Ministry's implementing agreement and prohibited-goods list due ~Aug 16, 2026 and enforcement beginning a further 30 days after that list is published -- neither published as of Aug 5)

Summary and Source: DGFT Notification No. 23/2026-27, New Delhi, dated 13th July 2026, was verified directly against the primary document on August 6, 2026 (the PDF is an image-only scan with no text layer, which is why extraction failed on every earlier attempt; it was rendered and read visually). Verified from the document: headed "To be published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part-II, Section-3, Sub-Section (ii)," issued under Section 3 read with Section 5 of the Foreign Trade (Development & Regulation) Act, 1992 and paragraphs 1.02 and 2.01 of FTP 2023, signed by Lav Agarwal, Director General of Foreign Trade and Addl. Secretary, File No. K-31013/1/2026-DIR NAFTA-Part(4). New Para 2.20B reads: "The import of goods produced or manufactured, wholly or in part, through the use of forced labour is prohibited. The Central Government may, from time to time, specify, by notification, the goods whose import shall be prohibited under this paragraph, having regard to the findings of such enquiry or such other material as it may consider appropriate. The procedure for conducting an enquiry by the Director General of Foreign Trade into the use of forced labour in the production of such goods shall be as prescribed in the Handbook of Procedures, 2023." New Para 11.64 defines "Forced Labour" per ILO Convention No. 29. The first sentence of Para 2.20B is a flat self-executing prohibition; the notification power goes to designating specific goods, structurally similar to Trinidad and Tobago's designation-dependent ban. EFFECTIVE DATE, narrowed this run but still not settled: the text ties effect to "the expiry of 30 days from the date of publication of this Notification in the Official Gazette," and DGFT's own notification index (dgft.gov.in) lists this notification with a notification date of 13/07/2026 and a portal posting timestamp of 14/07/2026 15:00:59. That brackets the issuance and public release but is DGFT's own site, not the Gazette of India, so the Gazette publication date that actually starts the 30-day clock remains unconfirmed and the widely cited ~August 12, 2026 effective date is still an inference rather than a verified figure. No banned-goods list, trade notice or Handbook of Procedures amendment has been published. Source: DGFT Notification No. 23/2026-27 (primary document, read directly); DGFT notification index, dgft.gov.in; corroborated by Taxscan, The Wire, Business Standard and an ELP legal alert.

Summary and Source: Malaysia's 10% tier rests on its US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (signed October 2025), which Minister Johari Abdul Ghani confirmed on July 25, 2026 is signed but not ratified -- the 2-year clock to legislate a forced-labour import ban starts only on ratification. Summary and Source: New Zealand rejects USTR's findings -- Prime Minister Christopher Luxon called the 12.5% tariff "extremely disappointing" and said the investigation "did not provide meaningful evidence" of forced labour, and Trade Minister Todd McClay called the process "not rigorous" while confirming NZ will not retaliate. PRECISION CORRECTION this run: this row previously stated that the Council of Ministers did not approve that request at its August 5 session. That overstated the sourcing. Summary and Source: Taiwan's 10%-tier eligibility rests on its February 12, 2026 US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, under which Taiwan committed to prohibit forced-labor-produced imports. INSTRUMENT NOW ISSUED: on July 30, 2026 the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Ministry of Labor jointly issued the "Operating Guidelines for Restricting the Import of Forced Labor Goods" and a companion "Review Committee Establishment Guidelines," under Article 11 of the Foreign Trade Act -- the administrative instrument previously recorded here as forthcoming. A 12-member review committee co-chaired by the MOEA and MOL ministers must decide within 30 days of receiving a forced-labour referral, after which the competent authority publishes a notice restricting or lifting the import restriction, with Customs and the Finance Ministry notifying importers to return or destroy listed goods. Column 6 accordingly upgraded to Taiwan's own Ministry of Labor announcement. Classification remains Partial on the same reasoning applied to the Philippines' Joint Administrative Order: this is an enforcement regime under existing statutory authority, not a standalone enacted import prohibition, and no Legislative Yuan bill has been tabled (the separate Employment Service Act amendments address labour brokerage, not imports). Source: Ministry of Labor (Taiwan, official), July 30, 2026; Newtalk and Taipei Times, July 30-31, 2026; USTR fact sheet, February 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (US-Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, February 12, 2026 treaty commitment, now implemented through MOEA/MOL Operating Guidelines and a Review Committee issued July 30, 2026 under Foreign Trade Act Art. 11; still an administrative regime under existing authority -- no statutory import prohibition enacted and no Legislative Yuan bill tabled)

Summary and Source: The specific domestic instrument has now been located and verified directly: Trinidad and Tobago's Finance Act, 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), assented to on 25 June 2026 and published in Legal Supplement Part A to the Trinidad and Tobago Gazette, Vol. 65, No. 111, 29 June 2026, section 24 amends the Customs Act (Chap. 78:01) section 45(1) by inserting a new paragraph: "(w) all goods produced from forced labour as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade". Section 45(1) is the Customs Act's list of prohibited/restricted imports, so this is a genuine, enacted, gazetted forced-labor import prohibition (designation-dependent -- the specific list of goods is left to the Minister with responsibility for trade to designate, similar in structure to several other economies' framework-style bans). This confirms and supersedes the prior entry's reliance on USTR's Federal Register final-action notice (which had stated, without naming the instrument, that Trinidad and Tobago "adopt[ed] a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN" -- the Finance Act's 25 June 2026 assent date fits neatly within that window). USTR's final action (July 23, 2026) placed Trinidad and Tobago in the 10% tariff tier on this basis. Source: Trinidad and Tobago e-Gazette (printery.gov.tt), Finance Act 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), 29 June 2026; USTR Federal Register final-action notice, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Finance Act, 2026, Act No. 16 of 2026, assented 25 June 2026, gazetted 29 June 2026, section 24 amends Customs Act Chap. 78:01 s.45(1) by adding paragraph (w) prohibiting the importation of goods produced from forced labour, as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade -- a framework-style ban pending ministerial designation of the specific goods list)

Summary and Source: USTR credited the UK with a "partial regime" (2023 Procurement Act forced-labour exclusions, 2025 Great British Energy Act provisions), securing the 10% tier. No government import-ban bill has been tabled: bills.parliament.uk shows only the Import of Products of Forced Labour from Xinjiang (Prohibition) Bill, a narrow private member's bill; the Joint Committee on Human Rights report and the Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner's December 2025 "model legislative drafting" report are advisory; and the Employment Rights Act 2025 (Fair Work Agency) is domestic enforcement, not an import measure. NEW this run: the JCHR's "Forced Labour in UK Supply Chains" report is scheduled for debate in the House of Lords on September 4, 2026, and a government written answer in July 2026 said it is "considering the review's findings" -- both still deliberative, neither a tabled measure. Trade Minister Chris Bryant said on June 30, 2026 that government is still debating design and enforcement but hopes to legislate before this Parliament ends (~2029). STALE/FALSE-POSITIVE GUARD: search results have surfaced a claim that the government "introduced a bill on June 30, 2026" -- that traces to the Business and Trade Committee hearing at which Bryant made those remarks, NOT to any bill introduction, and no such bill appears on the parliamentary register. Do not treat it as a tabled government measure. Source: UK Parliament (bills.parliament.uk) and House of Lords Library; Independent Anti-Slavery Commissioner, December 2025; Export Compliance Daily, July 1, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (procurement exclusions + Modern Slavery Act reporting; no full import prohibition and no government import-ban bill tabled -- only a limited private member's bill and advisory reports, with the JCHR report due for Lords debate September 4, 2026)

Summary and Source: Juan Labraga, director of the Trade Policy Advisory office at Uruguay's Ministry of Economy and Finance, traveled to Washington in late May 2026 for confidential technical consultations with USTR on Uruguay's import-control procedures; the Ministry views the forced-labor standard as "a new requirement that is here to stay" and is documenting compliance, while evaluating joining other economies in challenging the USTR findings. Source: La Mañana (Uruguay), 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Uruguay, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No

Summary and Source: Vietnam's Government issued Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP on July 22, 2026, implementing the Law on Foreign Trade Management; item 23 of its Appendix I prohibited-import list bans "products and goods extracted, produced, or manufactured wholly or partly through forced labor." Effective September 5, 2026 (45 days after issuance). Vietnam's Foreign Ministry separately rejected USTR's findings and reiterated that Vietnam "strictly prohibits all forms of forced labour." IMPLEMENTATION STATUS re-checked in Vietnamese on August 6, 2026, one month before the decree bites: still no implementing circular (thong tu), no General Department of Customs preparation notice, and none of the ministry-level HS-code-level goods lists the decree requires. Note the decree predated USTR's July 23 final determination by one day yet Vietnam was still placed in the 12.5% tier. Source: Bao Chinh Phu (Vietnam Government Portal), July 22, 2026; Lao Dong; Thoi Bao Ngan Hang and LuatVietnam, July 22-23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decree No. 292/2026/ND-CP, issued July 22, 2026, Appendix I item 23; effective September 5, 2026, with implementing circular and ministry-level HS-code goods lists still unpublished as of Aug 6)
